title: Single-particle Bloch bundles and band topology

items.title: Lattice Bloch transform and band projectors
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Let $d,r\ge1$ be integers, let $S\subset\mathbb Z^d$ be finite with $S=-S$, and let $T_\delta\in M_r(\mathbb C)$ satisfy $T_{-\delta}=T_\delta^*$ for each $\delta\in S$. Give $\mathbb C^r$ its standard Hermitian inner product, conjugate-linear in the first variable, and set $\mathcal H=\ell^2(\mathbb Z^d;\mathbb C^r)$ with the sum inner product. On finitely supported $\psi\in\mathcal H$ define

$$ (H_0\psi)_n=\sum_{\delta\in S}T_\delta\psi_{n-\delta}. $$

Let $\mathbb T^d_{2\pi}:=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized Haar measure $(2\pi)^{-d}dk$ and orientation $dk_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dk_d$. On finitely supported sequences define

$$ (\mathcal F_0\psi)(k)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z^d}\psi_n e^{-ik\cdot n},\qquad h(k)=\sum_{\delta\in S}T_\delta e^{-ik\cdot\delta}. $$

Assume Countable Choice for the unitary-extension assertion. The **finite-range lattice Bloch model** is the bounded extension $H$ of $H_0$, together with the unitary extension $\mathcal F$ of $\mathcal F_0$ and its finite-matrix fibers $h(k)$. An **isolated band cluster of rank $m$** is a fixed nonempty consecutive block of $m$ eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, of the Hermitian matrix $h(k)$ whose distance from the complementary eigenvalues is bounded below by a single $\gamma>0$ for all $k$; if the block is the full spectrum, its projector is $I_r$. The **band projector** $P(k)$ is the orthogonal projection onto the sum of the eigenspaces in that block. For $d=2$, $\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}$ is the oriented Brillouin torus used on this page.

This definition concerns finite-range hopping on a discrete lattice. It does not identify that model with a continuum periodic Schrödinger operator.

references.title: János K. Asbóth, László Oroszlány, and András Pályi, A Short Course on Topological Insulators
David Tong, Applications of Quantum Mechanics, University of Cambridge lecture notes

items.title: Exact Bloch transform and regularity of gapped band projectors
items.design_state: Scaffolder-added local A-page prerequisite; complete definition or proof is authored in this batch.
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and the data of [[def-nrqmx-bloch-fiber-model]]. The finite-range operator $H_0$ extends uniquely to a bounded self-adjoint operator $H$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^d;\mathbb C^r)$, and $\mathcal F_0$ extends uniquely to a unitary map $\mathcal F:\mathcal H\to L^2(\mathbb T^d_{2\pi};\mathbb C^r)$. For every $k$, $h(k)$ is Hermitian, $\|h(k)\|\le\sum_{\delta\in S}\|T_\delta\|$, and

$$ (\mathcal F H\mathcal F^{-1}f)(k)=h(k)f(k) $$

as an equality in $L^2$. The matrix family $h$ is $C^\infty$. If a nonempty consecutive eigenvalue block is separated from its complement by a uniform gap $\gamma>0$, its orthogonal spectral projector $P(k)$ is $C^\infty$ and is locally the Riesz projection

$$ P(k)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_\Gamma(zI-h(k))^{-1}\,dz, $$

where $\Gamma$ is a fixed finite union of positively oriented circles separating the selected eigenvalues from the others on the neighborhood in question.

references.title: János K. Asbóth, László Oroszlány, and András Pályi, A Short Course on Topological Insulators
David Tong, Applications of Quantum Mechanics, University of Cambridge lecture notes

items.proof_route: Bound the finite hopping operator; identify the Fourier synthesis unitary and multiplication fibers; prove smoothness of the gapped Riesz projector locally.
items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F4], and the data in the Definition.

1.1 For finitely supported $\psi$, each shift $\psi_n\mapsto\psi_{n-\delta}$ preserves the $\ell^2$ norm, so the triangle inequality gives $\|H_0\psi\|_2\le(\sum_{\delta\in S}\|T_\delta\|)\|\psi\|_2$. Hence $H_0$ extends uniquely to a bounded operator $H$. For finitely supported $\psi,\phi$, reindexing the finite sum gives $\langle H_0\psi,\phi\rangle=\sum_{m,\delta}\langle T_\delta\psi_m,\phi_{m+\delta}\rangle=\sum_{m,\delta}\langle\psi_m,T_\delta^*\phi_{m+\delta}\rangle=\langle\psi,H_0\phi\rangle$, because $T_\delta^*=T_{-\delta}$ and $S=-S$. Density and boundedness extend symmetry to all of $\mathcal H$, so $H=H^*$. [given, algebra]

1.2 Under $k=2\pi x$, the functions $e^{-ik\cdot n}$ are the characters $e_{-n}(x)$. By [F1] and [F2], applied to each of the finitely many internal coordinates, $\mathcal F_0$ preserves the $L^2$ norm and its range contains the dense trigonometric polynomials; it therefore has a unique isometric extension $\mathcal F$, and the completeness clause of [F1] makes that extension onto. Thus $\mathcal F$ is unitary. [A1, F1, F2, given]

1.3 Direct substitution and the change of index $m=n-\delta$ give, for finitely supported $\psi$, $\mathcal F_0(H_0\psi)(k)=\sum_{\delta\in S}T_\delta e^{-ik\cdot\delta}\sum_m\psi_m e^{-ik\cdot m}=h(k)\mathcal F_0\psi(k)$. The finite sum defining $h$ is continuous and satisfies $\sup_k\|h(k)\|\le\sum_{\delta\in S}\|T_\delta\|$, so multiplication by $h$ is bounded on $L^2$. Extending the identity from the dense finitely supported sequences proves the claimed unitary equivalence. Also, $h(k)^*=\sum_\delta T_\delta^*e^{ik\cdot\delta}=\sum_\delta T_{-\delta}e^{-ik\cdot(-\delta)}=h(k)$, and its entries are trigonometric polynomials, hence smooth. [given, algebra]

1.4 Write the eigenvalues of $h(k)$ in nondecreasing order as $\lambda_1(k)\le\cdots\le\lambda_r(k)$. For a Hermitian matrix $A$ with eigenbasis $e_1,\ldots,e_r$, its $j$th eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda_j(A)=\max_{\dim L=r-j+1}\min_{\|v\|=1,\,v\in L}\langle Av,v\rangle$: every such $L$ intersects $\operatorname{span}(e_1,\ldots,e_j)$ nontrivially, while $L=\operatorname{span}(e_j,\ldots,e_r)$ attains the value. Since every unit-vector Rayleigh quotient changes by at most $\|A-B\|$ when $A$ is replaced by $B$, this formula gives $|\lambda_j(A)-\lambda_j(B)|\le\|A-B\|$. Thus each $\lambda_j(k)$ is continuous. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix $k_0$. The gap and continuity in step 1.4 let us choose disjoint small circles around the distinct eigenvalues in the selected block at $k_0$ so that, on some neighborhood of $k_0$, all selected eigenvalues stay inside their union and all complementary eigenvalues stay outside. The inverse matrix $(zI-h(k))^{-1}$ is $C^\infty$ in $k$ on this fixed contour: differentiating the inverse gives $\partial_j(zI-h)^{-1}=(zI-h)^{-1}(\partial_jh)(zI-h)^{-1}$, and repeated differentiation gives finite sums of products of smooth matrices. Therefore its contour integral is $C^\infty$. At each $k$, [F3] diagonalizes $h(k)$, and [F4] evaluates the contour integral on each eigenvector, proving that it is exactly the orthogonal projector onto the selected eigenvalues. On overlaps the local definitions project onto the same selected eigenspaces, so they agree and define the asserted global projector. [F3, F4, step 1.4, given, algebra] ∎

items.title: Determinant line and its projector
items.design_state: Scaffolder-added local A-page prerequisite; complete definition or proof is authored in this batch.
items.statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $r\ge1$, and let $P:M\to M_r(\mathbb C)$ be a $C^2$ orthogonal projector of constant rank $m$, with $1\le m\le r$. Its image bundle is $E_P=\{(x,v):P(x)v=v\}$, with the projected connection $\nabla s=P\,ds$ of [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]]. The **determinant line bundle** is the complex line bundle

$$\det E_P:=\bigwedge^m E_P\subset M\times\bigwedge^m\mathbb C^r.$$

Give $\bigwedge^m\mathbb C^r$ the Hermitian inner product for which $e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_m}$, $i_1<\cdots<i_m$, is an orthonormal basis, where $(e_1,\ldots,e_r)$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb C^r$. The **determinant-line projector** at $x$ is $Q(x):=\bigwedge^m P(x)$; it is the orthogonal projection onto $\bigwedge^m\operatorname{im}P(x)$.

references.title: Keith Conrad, Exterior Powers

items.title: The determinant-line projector is smooth and rank one
items.design_state: Scaffolder-added local A-page prerequisite; complete definition or proof is authored in this batch.
items.statement: For the projector of [[def-nrqmx-determinant-line-projector]], $Q(x)=\bigwedge^mP(x)$ is a $C^2$ orthogonal projector of rank one. Its range is exactly $\det E_P(x)=\bigwedge^m\operatorname{im}P(x)$, so these ranges form the determinant line bundle.

references.title: Keith Conrad, Exterior Powers

items.proof_route: Use minors and exterior functoriality to prove the induced map is a smooth rank-one orthogonal projector onto the determinant line.
items.strategy:
**Given:** [F1]–[F5].

1.1 In the standard orthonormal wedge basis from [F4], the matrix entry of $\bigwedge^m T$ in row $I$, column $J$ is $\det T_{I,J}$ by [F3]. Consequently $[(\bigwedge^mT)^*]_{I,J}=\overline{\det T_{J,I}}=\det (T^*)_{I,J}$, so $(\bigwedge^mT)^*=\bigwedge^m(T^*)$. Applying this to $P=P^*$ shows $Q=Q^*$. [F1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Functoriality [F2] gives $Q^2=\bigwedge^m(P^2)=\bigwedge^mP=Q$. Hence $Q$ is a Hermitian idempotent by step 1.1; for $x=Qy$ and $Qz=0$, $\langle x,z\rangle=\langle Qy,z\rangle=\langle y,Qz\rangle=0$, so its range and kernel are orthogonal and it is the orthogonal projection onto its range. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Every decomposable wedge in the image of $Q$ is a wedge of $m$ vectors in $\operatorname{im}P$, so the full image lies in $\bigwedge^m\operatorname{im}P$. Conversely, for a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_m$ of the $m$-dimensional range of $P$, $Q(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m)=v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m\ne0$. The increasing-wedge basis theorem [F4], applied to this basis of the range, says $\bigwedge^m\operatorname{im}P$ is one-dimensional; thus it equals $\operatorname{im}Q$ and $Q$ has rank one. [F2, F4, step 2.1]

4.1 Each matrix entry of $Q(x)$ is a polynomial minor in the entries of $P(x)$ by [F3], hence is $C^2$. Together with step 2.1 this proves that $Q$ is a $C^2$ rank-one orthogonal projector with the stated range, and its ranges form the determinant line subbundle. [F3, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

items.title: Determinant-line curvature is the trace curvature
items.design_state: Scaffolder-added local A-page prerequisite; complete definition or proof is authored in this batch.
items.statement:
Let $P$ be a $C^2$ rank-$m$ orthogonal projector and let $F=P(dP\wedge dP)P$ be the curvature of its projected connection. On any open set with a $C^2$ orthonormal frame $V=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)$, put $A=V^*dV$ and $w=v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m$. The induced projected connection on $\det E_P$ has local connection one-form $a=\operatorname{tr}A$ in the unit frame $w$, and its scalar curvature is

$$da=\operatorname{tr}(V^*FV)=\operatorname{tr}F.$$

Thus the curvature of the determinant line is the trace of the original bundle curvature, with the same orientation and sign convention.

references.title: Di Xiao, Ming-Che Chang, and Qian Niu, Berry Phase Effects on Electronic Properties
references.locator: Section I.C and Appendix A, projector curvature and connection conventions.

items.proof_route: Compute the determinant connection in a local wedge frame and show its scalar curvature equals the trace of the bundle curvature.
items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F3].

1.1 Because the columns of $V$ are orthonormal, $w=v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m$ has unit norm and spans the determinant line. Differentiating by the product rule gives $dw=\sum_j v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dv_j\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m$. The projected connection applies $P$ to each differentiated factor. Since $P\,dv_j=\sum_a v_a A_{aj}$, each term with $a\ne j$ vanishes from a repeated wedge factor, while the $a=j$ term is $A_{jj}w$. Summing gives $Qdw=(\operatorname{tr}A)w$, so the determinant connection form is $a=\operatorname{tr}A$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 A line connection with scalar one-form $a$ has curvature $da+a\wedge a=da$, since a scalar one-form wedges with itself to zero. By [F3], $\operatorname{tr}F=\operatorname{tr}(dA)+\operatorname{tr}(A\wedge A)$. In coordinates, $\operatorname{tr}(A\wedge A)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\wedge A_{ji}=0$: diagonal terms vanish and each off-diagonal pair cancels because one-forms anticommute. Therefore $da=d\operatorname{tr}A=\operatorname{tr}F_{\mathrm{fr}}=\operatorname{tr}(V^*FV)$. Finally, since $PFP=F$ and $VV^*=P$, cyclicity of finite-dimensional trace gives $\operatorname{tr}(V^*FV)=\operatorname{tr}(FVV^*)=\operatorname{tr}(FP)=\operatorname{tr}F$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Normalized area integral equals the degree
items.design_state: Scaffolder-added local A-page prerequisite; complete definition or proof is authored in this batch.
items.statement:
Orient the unit sphere $S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$ outward and let $\omega_{S^2}$ be its normalized area form

$$\omega_{S^2}:=\frac{1}{4\pi}(x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy)\big|_{S^2},$$

so that $\int_{S^2}\omega_{S^2}=1$. For every smooth map $n:\mathbb T^2\to S^2$, where $\mathbb T^2$ has orientation $dk_1\wedge dk_2$, its integral degree satisfies

$$\int_{\mathbb T^2}n^*\omega_{S^2}=\deg(n)\in\mathbb Z.$$

Here degree is the integer determined by $n_*[\mathbb T^2]=\deg(n)[S^2]$ in integral homology.

references.title: Introduction to Differential Geometry: Manifolds, vector fields, and differential forms, University of Toronto course notes

items.proof_route: Use de Rham naturality, top-form fundamental-class evaluation, real-coefficient Kronecker naturality, and coefficient change of the integral degree equation.
items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [A2], [F1]–[F6], and $n$ as in the statement.

1.1 In spherical coordinates $x=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$, $z=\cos\theta$, the unnormalized displayed two-form is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. Integrating for $0\le\theta\le\pi$ and $0\le\phi\le2\pi$ gives $4\pi$, so $\omega_{S^2}$ is a smooth closed form with integral one; its displayed ambient expression shows it extends smoothly across the coordinate poles. [given, algebra]

2.1 Let $J$ be the natural comparison in [F3]. By [F5], $\int_{\mathbb T^2}n^*\omega_{S^2}=\langle J([n^*\omega_{S^2}]),[\mathbb T^2]_{\mathbb R}\rangle$. Naturality of $J$ and of the real-coefficient Kronecker pairing [F4] then gives $\int_{\mathbb T^2}n^*\omega_{S^2}=\langle J([\omega_{S^2}]),n_*[\mathbb T^2]_{\mathbb R}\rangle$. [A1, A2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], $n_*[\mathbb T^2]_{\mathbb Z}=\deg(n)[S^2]_{\mathbb Z}$. The coefficient map $\iota:C_\bullet(X;\mathbb Z)\to C_\bullet(X;\mathbb R)$ sends each finite sum $\sum_j a_j\sigma_j$ to $\sum_j a_j\sigma_j$ with the same coefficients viewed in $\mathbb R$. It commutes with boundaries because [F6] defines the singular boundary as an integer linear combination of faces and $\iota$ is additive; it commutes with $n_\#$ because [F6] postcomposes each simplex without changing its coefficient. Hence it induces a coefficient-change map on homology and carries each integral fundamental class to its real fundamental class: it sends the positive local orientation generator $1$ to $1$, so uniqueness of the class with those local restrictions in [F2] identifies the image. Applying $\iota$ to the degree equation gives $n_*[\mathbb T^2]_{\mathbb R}=\deg(n)[S^2]_{\mathbb R}$. By the real-coefficient bilinearity of [F4], step 2.1 becomes $\int_{\mathbb T^2}n^*\omega_{S^2}=\deg(n)\langle J([\omega_{S^2}]),[S^2]_{\mathbb R}\rangle=\deg(n)\int_{S^2}\omega_{S^2}=\deg(n)$ by [F5] and step 1.1. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Gapped band curvature and Chern invariance
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $P:\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}\to M_r(\mathbb C)$ be a $C^2$ orthogonal projector of constant rank $m\ge1$; in particular it may be the projector of an isolated band cluster of a finite-range Bloch Hamiltonian. Use the orientation $dk_1\wedge dk_2$, let $E_P=\operatorname{im}P$, and let $F=P(dP\wedge dP)P$ be the curvature of the projected connection $\nabla=P\,d$. Then

$$C(P):=\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb T^2}\operatorname{tr}F=\left\langle c_1(\det E_P),[\mathbb T^2]\right\rangle\in\mathbb Z.$$

For every jointly $C^2$ family $P_t$ of such projectors, $0\le t\le1$, with the same rank, $C(P_t)$ is independent of $t$. In particular this holds for a $C^2$ Bloch Hamiltonian deformation whose chosen spectral cluster retains a uniform gap. If $E_P$ has a global $C^2$ periodic orthonormal frame, then $C(P)=0$.

references.title: János K. Asbóth, László Oroszlány, and András Pályi, A Short Course on Topological Insulators
David Tong, Applications of Quantum Mechanics, University of Cambridge lecture notes
Di Xiao, Ming-Che Chang, and Qian Niu, Berry Phase Effects on Electronic Properties

items.proof_route: Pass to the determinant line, apply the rank-one Chern theorem, then prove homotopy invariance and the global-frame obstruction by continuity and Stokes.
items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [A2], [F1]–[F6].

1.1 For each fixed $t$ (or for the single projector), [F1] gives the rank-one projector $Q_t=\bigwedge^mP_t$ onto $\det E_{P_t}$. Its image is a complex line bundle over the compact torus, hence is numerable; the torus is a compact smooth CW complex. The determinant-line curvature lemma [F2] gives $\operatorname{tr}F_t=\operatorname{tr}(Q_t(dQ_t\wedge dQ_t)Q_t)$ pointwise, with the same orientation convention. Applying [F3] to $Q_t$ proves the displayed equality and integrality, with $c_1$ interpreted by [F5]. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F5, given]

2.1 For a jointly $C^2$ family, the coefficient function $g(k,t)$ of the two-form $\operatorname{tr}(P_t(dP_t\wedge dP_t)P_t)$ is continuous on the compact set $\mathbb T^2\times[0,1]$, so it is uniformly continuous. If $t_j\to t$, then $\sup_k|g(k,t_j)-g(k,t)|\to0$; therefore $C(P_{t_j})\to C(P_t)$ by bounding the difference of integrals by the torus's finite area times this supremum. Thus $t\mapsto C(P_t)$ is continuous. Step 1.1 makes it integer-valued, and a continuous integer-valued function on the connected interval $[0,1]$ is constant: otherwise the intermediate-value theorem would give a noninteger value between two distinct integer values. For a uniformly gapped Hamiltonian deformation, [F6] supplies the required joint $C^2$ spectral projectors by the local contour formula. [F2, F3, F6, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 If $V$ is a global $C^2$ periodic orthonormal frame, then $A=V^*dV$ is a globally defined $C^1$ matrix-valued one-form. By [F2] and its proof, $\operatorname{tr}F=d\operatorname{tr}A$ (the trace of $A\wedge A$ vanishes). Hence $C(P)=\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb T^2}d\operatorname{tr}A=0$ by [F4], since the torus has empty boundary. [F2, F4, given] ∎

items.title: Two-band Chern number and degree formula
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let a two-orbital finite-range Bloch Hamiltonian on the oriented torus $\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}$ have the form

$$h(k)=d_0(k)I+d_1(k)\sigma_1+d_2(k)\sigma_2+d_3(k)\sigma_3,$$

where $d_0,d_1,d_2,d_3$ are real smooth periodic functions, $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ are the Pauli matrices, and $d=(d_1,d_2,d_3)$ is nowhere zero. Define $n=d/|d|$. The upper and lower band projectors are $P_+=(I+n\cdot\sigma)/2$ and $P_-=(I-n\cdot\sigma)/2$. With the Chern convention $C(P)=(i/2\pi)\int_{\mathbb T^2}\operatorname{tr}(P(dP\wedge dP)P)$ and orientation $dk_1\wedge dk_2$,

$$C(P_+)=-\deg(n)=-\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb T^2}n\cdot(\partial_{k_1}n\times\partial_{k_2}n)\,dk_1\,dk_2,\qquad C(P_-)=+\deg(n)=+\frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb T^2}n\cdot(\partial_{k_1}n\times\partial_{k_2}n)\,dk_1\,dk_2.$$

references.title: János K. Asbóth, László Oroszlány, and András Pályi, A Short Course on Topological Insulators
David Tong, Applications of Quantum Mechanics, University of Cambridge lecture notes
Di Xiao, Ming-Che Chang, and Qian Niu, Berry Phase Effects on Electronic Properties

items.proof_route: Expand the projector curvature with Pauli identities and apply the normalized area-degree formula.
items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F3]. Write $s\in\{+1,-1\}$ for the upper or lower band sign.

1.1 Direct multiplication of the displayed Pauli matrices gives $\sigma_a\sigma_b=\delta_{ab}I+i\sum_c\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c$, $\operatorname{tr}\sigma_a=0$, and $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_a\sigma_b)=2\delta_{ab}$. Thus $(n\cdot\sigma)^2=|n|^2I=I$, and $h=d_0I+|d|(n\cdot\sigma)$ has eigenvalues $d_0\pm|d|$ with the stated orthogonal projectors. Since $|d|$ is continuous and positive on compact $\mathbb T^2$, its minimum is positive, so the two bands are uniformly separated; $n$ and $P_s$ are smooth. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Differentiating $P_s=(I+s n\cdot\sigma)/2$ gives $\partial_jP_s=(s/2)(\partial_jn)\cdot\sigma$. The Pauli product identity yields $[a\cdot\sigma,b\cdot\sigma]=2i(a\times b)\cdot\sigma$, hence $[\partial_1P_s,\partial_2P_s]=\frac{i}{2}(\partial_1n\times\partial_2n)\cdot\sigma$. Using $\operatorname{tr}(P_s\sigma_a)=s n_a$, which follows from the trace identities in step 1.1, we obtain $\operatorname{tr}(P_s[\partial_1P_s,\partial_2P_s])=\frac{i s}{2}n\cdot(\partial_1n\times\partial_2n)$. In dimension two this is the coefficient of $\operatorname{tr}(P_s(dP_s\wedge dP_s)P_s)$: cyclicity and $P_s^2=P_s$ give $\operatorname{tr}(P_sXP_s)=\operatorname{tr}(P_sX)$. Multiplying by $i/(2\pi)$ therefore gives $C(P_s)=-s(4\pi)^{-1}\int n\cdot(\partial_1n\times\partial_2n)\,dk_1dk_2$. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The normalized area form in [F3] pulls back to $(4\pi)^{-1}n\cdot(\partial_1n\times\partial_2n)\,dk_1\wedge dk_2$, by the defining outward area form on the unit sphere. Hence its integral is $\deg(n)$ by [F3]. Substitution into step 2.1 gives $C(P_s)=-s\deg(n)$, which is the two displayed upper- and lower-band formulas. [F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Conditional band velocity and anomalous term
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^3$ be an open coordinate chart of a three-dimensional Brillouin torus, let $h:U\to M_r(\mathbb C)$ be the restriction of a $C^2$ Hermitian finite-range Bloch fiber family, and let $\varepsilon:U\to\mathbb R$ be a simple eigenvalue with a positive local gap from the other eigenvalues. On a local chart choose a $C^2$ normalized eigenvector $u(k)$ for $\varepsilon(k)$. Under an adopted slow-force single-band effective description, for position $x\in\mathbb R^3$, crystal wave vector $k\in U$, constant signed charge $q$, constant electric field $\mathbf E_{\rm ext}$, and reduced Planck constant $\hbar>0$, take the effective Lagrangian

$$L=\hbar k\cdot\dot x+i\hbar\,u(k)^*\nabla_k u(k)\cdot\dot k-\varepsilon(k)+q\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\cdot x.$$

Here $k$ is measured in radians per metre, $x$ in metres, $\varepsilon$ in joules, $q$ in coulombs, $\mathbf E_{\rm ext}$ in volts per metre, and $\hbar$ in joule seconds. Let $\mathcal A(k):=i u(k)^*\nabla_k u(k)\in\mathbb R^3$ and $\boldsymbol\Omega(k):=\nabla_k\times\mathcal A(k)$. Every $C^2$ stationary curve of this adopted effective action satisfies

$$\hbar\dot k=q\mathbf E_{\rm ext},\qquad \dot x=\frac{1}{\hbar}\nabla_k\varepsilon-\dot k\times\boldsymbol\Omega.$$

The equations are invariant under a local phase change of $u$. This is the exact Euler–Lagrange consequence of the stated effective Lagrangian; it supplies no error estimate for replacing the underlying quantum dynamics by that Lagrangian.

For a two-band specialization, the normalization of $\boldsymbol\Omega$ agrees with the Chern convention of the two-band degree formula.

references.title: Di Xiao, Ming-Che Chang, and Qian Niu, Berry Phase Effects on Electronic Properties
references.locator: Sections III.A and V.A, Eqs. (3.6)–(3.7) and (5.7)–(5.8).

references.title: David Tong, Applications of Quantum Mechanics, University of Cambridge lecture notes

items.proof_route: Treat the stated Lagrangian as adopted, check gauge covariance, and derive both equations by coordinatewise Euler–Lagrange differentiation.
items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [A2], [F1], [F2], a local normalized eigenvector, and the variables and constants in the statement.

1.1 Differentiating $u^*u=1$ gives $(\partial_j u)^*u+u^*\partial_j u=0$, so $u^*\partial_j u$ is purely imaginary and $\mathcal A_j=i u^*\partial_j u$ is real. If only the smooth rank-one projector $P(k)$ is given, fix a unit vector $v\in\operatorname{im}P(k_0)$; by continuity $P(k)v\ne0$ near $k_0$, and $u(k)=P(k)v/\|P(k)v\|$ supplies the required local $C^2$ normalized section. Under $u'=e^{i\chi}u$, direct differentiation gives $\mathcal A'=\mathcal A-\nabla_k\chi$, so $\boldsymbol\Omega'=\boldsymbol\Omega$ and the Lagrangian changes by $-\hbar\,d\chi/dt$, a total derivative. Thus the equations are chart independent. [A1, A2, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For each coordinate $x_j$, $\partial L/\partial\dot x_j=\hbar k_j$ and $\partial L/\partial x_j=q(E_{\rm ext})_j$. The Euler–Lagrange equation $\frac{d}{dt}(\partial L/\partial\dot x_j)-\partial L/\partial x_j=0$ therefore gives $\hbar\dot k_j=q(E_{\rm ext})_j$, the first vector equation. [A1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.2 For each $k_j$, $\partial L/\partial\dot k_j=\hbar\mathcal A_j$ and $\partial L/\partial k_j=\hbar\dot x_j+\hbar\sum_i(\partial_j\mathcal A_i)\dot k_i-\partial_j\varepsilon$. Applying Euler–Lagrange and the chain rule gives $\hbar\dot x_j=\partial_j\varepsilon+\hbar\sum_i(\partial_i\mathcal A_j-\partial_j\mathcal A_i)\dot k_i=\partial_j\varepsilon-\hbar(\dot k\times\boldsymbol\Omega)_j$, where the last equality is the component identity $\partial_i\mathcal A_j-\partial_j\mathcal A_i=-\epsilon_{j i\ell}(\nabla_k\times\mathcal A)_\ell$. Dividing by $\hbar>0$ gives the second vector equation. [A1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

2.3 On a two-band chart with $P_s=u u^*$, direct differentiation of $P_s$ gives $\Omega_{12}=i\,\operatorname{tr}(P_s[\partial_1P_s,\partial_2P_s])$. Thus $(2\pi)^{-1}\int\Omega_{12}=C(P_s)$ in the projector convention, and [F2] gives its signed degree value; this confirms that the anomalous term uses the same sign convention as the preceding band formula. The variational derivation itself does not depend on a two-band restriction. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The result is the Euler–Lagrange consequence of the adopted finite-dimensional effective Lagrangian. It does not establish that a physical wave packet follows these equations, nor quantify any error from neglected interband transitions or higher spatial and temporal derivatives of the field. [A2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3] ∎

title: Single-particle Bloch bundles and band topology — Examples

items.title: Gap closings and Chern regions in the two-band lattice model
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement:
Assume Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For $M\in\mathbb R$, consider the two-orbital finite-range Bloch Hamiltonian

$$h_M(k)=\sin k_1\,\sigma_1+\sin k_2\,\sigma_2+(M+\cos k_1+\cos k_2)\,\sigma_3,$$

on the oriented torus $\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}$. Its spectral gap closes exactly when $M\in\{-2,0,2\}$. For each fixed $M$ outside this set, the lower and upper band Chern numbers in the convention $C(P)=\frac{i}{2\pi}\int\operatorname{tr}(P(dP\wedge dP)P)$ are

| Parameter range | $\deg(n_M)$ | $C(P_-)$ | $C(P_+)$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $M<-2$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $-2<M<0$ | $+1$ | $+1$ | $-1$ |
| $0<M<2$ | $-1$ | $-1$ | $+1$ |
| $M>2$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |

Each Chern number is constant on its parameter interval. At the three closing values a separated band projector, and therefore its Chern number, is not defined.

references.title: János K. Asbóth, László Oroszlány, and András Pályi, A Short Course on Topological Insulators
Di Xiao, Ming-Che Chang, and Qian Niu, Berry Phase Effects on Electronic Properties

items.proof_route: Solve the three-component gap equation and count signed north-pole preimages in each parameter region.
items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [F1], [F2], the Bloch matrix, and the standard orientations on the torus and sphere.

1.1 Write $d_M=(\sin k_1,\sin k_2,M+\cos k_1+\cos k_2)$. The band energies are $\pm|d_M|$, so the gap is $2|d_M|$ and closes exactly if all three components vanish. The first two vanish only when each $k_j$ is $0$ or $\pi$ modulo $2\pi$; the third component at $(0,0),(\pi,0),(0,\pi),(\pi,\pi)$ is respectively $M+2,M,M,M-2$. Thus a zero exists exactly at $M=-2,0,2$. For every other fixed $M$, compactness of the torus and continuity give $\min_k|d_M(k)|>0$, so the two bands have a uniform gap. The sine and cosine terms are finite Fourier sums with nearest-neighbor support, hence this is a finite-range Hermitian Bloch matrix. [given, algebra]

2.1 Fix $M$ outside the closing set and let $N=(0,0,1)\in S^2$. The preimages of $N$ under $n_M=d_M/|d_M|$ are exactly the four candidate points above for which the third component is positive. Near such a point, use the oriented coordinates $(n_1,n_2)$ at $N$. The derivative matrix is diagonal with entries $\cos k_1/d_3$ and $\cos k_2/d_3$, where $d_3=M+\cos k_1+\cos k_2>0$; its determinant is nonzero. Therefore $N$ is a regular value, and the local orientation signs at $(0,0),(\pi,0),(0,\pi),(\pi,\pi)$, whenever present, are respectively $+1,-1,-1,+1$. By [F2], degree is the sum of the signs for those points with $d_3>0$. [F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 If $M<-2$, no candidate has $d_3>0$ and the sum is $0$. If $-2<M<0$, only $(0,0)$ contributes, giving $+1$. If $0<M<2$, $(0,0),(\pi,0),(0,\pi)$ contribute $+1-1-1=-1$. If $M>2$, all four contribute $+1-1-1+1=0$. Substitution into [F1] gives every table entry. For any two values in one of the four intervals, the closed segment between them remains in that interval; the joint function $|d_M(k)|$ is positive on the compact torus times that segment, so it has a positive minimum and supplies a gap-preserving deformation. [A1, F1, step 2.1, given, algebra] ∎

items.title: A nonzero-Chern band has no global smooth periodic frame
items.design_state: Assigned design item; complete current statement and argument are recorded in its item carrier.
items.statement: Every smooth isolated Bloch band on the two-torus admits a global smooth periodic normalized eigenvector.

references.title: János K. Asbóth, László Oroszlány, and András Pályi, A Short Course on Topological Insulators
David Tong, Applications of Quantum Mechanics, University of Cambridge lecture notes

items.proof_route: Use the nonzero Chern number at M=1 to contradict the vanishing forced by a global normalized frame.
items.strategy:
**Given:** [A1], [F1], [F2], and the lower band of the stated two-band Hamiltonian at $M=1$. Its spectral gap is open and its Chern number is $-1$.

1.1 By [F1], this is a smooth rank-one orthogonal band projector with $C(P_-)=-1\ne0$. Suppose it had a global smooth periodic normalized eigenvector $u(k)$. Since its range is one-dimensional, $u(k)$ would be a global orthonormal frame of the line bundle. [A1, F1, given]

2.1 Apply [F2] to that frame: it would force $C(P_-)=0$, contradicting step 1.1's value $-1$. Thus this smooth isolated band has no global smooth periodic normalized eigenvector, refuting the universal statement. [F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
